newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian ANZ job ads rise 1.8 pct in Feb.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian ANZ job ads rise 1.8 pct in Feb.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group (ANZ) said on Tuesday its job advertisement series for February rose a seasonally adjusted 1.8 percent, following on a 3.3 percent rise in January.

Job ads had now risen in three of the past four months, and were at their highest level since July last year, the bank said. Compared with February last year, ANZ said the number of jobs ads was down 8.2 percent, which was the smallest decline over a 12 month period since March 1996.
In trend terms, the number of job ads rose 0.5 percent, the third consecutive increase following 21 months of continuous trend decline, ANZ said.
"An upturn in the demand for labour now seems to be clearly underway," ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake said in a statement.
Eslake said the recent trends in job ads were consistent with jobs growth of around 12,000 a month over the next three months.

Given the official employment data had shown faster growth than this over the past few months, "12,000 jobs per month over the remainder of the 1996/97 financial year would be just sufficient to achieve the government's forecast of 1.5 percent growth in employment for the year as a whole," Eslake said.
If the participation rate remained around its January level of 63.8 percent, 12,000 new jobs per month would see the unemployment rate stabilize at around 8.5 percent, he said.
"At this stage, however, the trend in employment advertising is not sufficiently strong to warrant expectations of an early or significant decline in the unemployment rate," Eslake said.

ANZ said the reason that employment had been stronger than expected over recent months, given the job advertisement series trends, was that part-time employment had accounted for virtually all employment since last July.
In contrast, between the employment trough in March 1993 and July last year, part-time jobs had accounted for only 40 percent of total employment growth.
ANZ said the job ads series correlates much better with full-time employment, which may be because part-time vacancies were more likely to be filled informally, without using advertising.
Job ads rose in every state during February except Western Australia, where they fell 3.2 percent.

"The underlying trend in recent months has been strongest in the Australian Captial Territory, Victoria, Western Australia and New South Wales and weakest in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania," the ANZ said.
Official labour force data for February is due on Thursday.
